children: 0508 GMT - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's comments at Jackson Hole reinforced the Fed's commitment to the 2% PCE inflation target, and the market responded by assigning a higher probability to rate hikes down the road, Madison Investments' Mike Sanders says in a note. "Warsh appears focused on using the Fed funds rate as the primary policy tool, keeping the Fed focused on the front end of the yield curve while the Treasury deals with other parts of the curve," the head of fixed income says. If the Fed is going to raise rates sometime in the next three to six months, that is already reflected to some degree in the five- to seven-year part of the curve, where real yields remain attractive, Sanders says. The PCE indicator is the Fed's preferred gauge of inflation. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0501 GMT - Bitcoin edges lower in Asia, staying below $80,000 as rate-hike expectations weigh. It's going to be a cautious few weeks for Bitcoin ahead of the Fed's next meeting, where markets are pricing a 25bp hike at about 65%, says IG's Tony Sycamore. One hike in isolation should not be a gamechanger as Bitcoin looks to build on its August rally, the analyst says. But two or three might be, and at this point IG sees about 60bp of Fed rate hikes priced by June 2027. From a technical perspective, dips back into the mid-to-low $70s will likely be well-supported, says Sycamore. A sustained break above the $81,500/$83,000 resistance area will be needed to signal that a move toward $95,000-$100,000 is underway. Bitcoin slip 0.2% to $78,725. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0443 GMT - Australia building approvals for new homes fell by 3.6% in July 2026, led by a 4.5% fall in private house approvals, as the fallout from higher interest rates and tax increases on property investors continues to be felt, the Housing Industry Association's senior economist, Tom Devitt says. New home building activity had good momentum heading into 2026, but higher rates, tax changes, global conflict and surging fuel costs, has interrupted the expansion, he adds. The headwinds appear set to reduce the supply of new homes, and lead to a worsening in affordability, he adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0428 GMT - Thailand's economic data in July points toward a sequential 3Q recovery, BofA Global Research economists say in a report. Growth slowed to 1.9% on year in 2Q, from 1Q's 2.8% expansion, amid rising energy prices. However, the economy improved on the demand and production side in July, driven by the ongoing artificial intelligence capital expenditure cycle, the easing Middle East conflict and government stimulus measures. Still, BofA warns that the growth recovery could be subdued, as many economic activities are import-intensive and would weigh on the current account and trade balance.(amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0403 GMT - Downward momentum in Australia house prices has become the dominating market factor, and risks of an "overshoot" in the extent of falls is rising, especially if interest rates rise further, says Matthew Hassan, head of Australia macro forecasting at Westpac. Seasonal effects will turn positive in coming months but, on their own, these are unlikely to act as a market circuit breaker, he adds. Buyers will have the upper hand in most markets heading into the southern hemisphere's spring. Even allowing for seasonality, prices in the biggest market of Sydney tracked a 15-20% annualized pace of decline in the past three months, he notes. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0402 GMT - China's enormous domestic savings are weighing on government bond yields, Barclays economists say in a research note. While the yield on U.S. 10-year Treasurys is at 4.78%, China's 10-year government bond yield sits at only 1.69%. The core difference lies in who buys the bonds, they note. The U.S. Treasury market depends on external buyers such as foreign central banks, sovereign wealth funds and Japanese life insurers. However, China's bond market is funded entirely by domestic savings, which are at 43% of its GDP, they note. The vast amount of savings are unable to flow abroad given capital controls and there are few attractive alternatives, Barclays says. "As a result, they end up in the bond market, even at very low yields," the bank adds. (sherry.qin@wsj.com)

0340 GMT - More developed Southeast Asian countries--such as Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam and the Philippines-- are likely to remain base of production over the next decade, for not just western multinational companies but also Chinese firms, DBS economists say in report. That's because manufacturers want redundancy in their production networks and lower concentration risks. Also these countries remain cost competitive and have potential for growth since they "offer a growing middle class, incomes that are bound to expand over time and a relatively young population," DBS says.(amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0318 GMT - India's growth momentum could ease over the next two quarters as government capex spending slows after being front-loaded early in the fiscal year, Goldman Sachs says in a note. "We bake in some sequential moderation...as central government capex growth is likely to decline after front-loading in the first four months of the fiscal year," economists Santanu Sengupta and Arjun Varma write. They note fixed-investment growth reached a four-year high of 11.9% in the April-June quarter and contributed around 4 percentage points to GDP growth. Net exports also provided a further three-point boost as exports surged and imports contracted. GS expects these drivers to moderate sequentially, though strong recent data prompt it to raise its 2026 growth forecast to 7.6% from 7.3%. (jihye.lee@wsj.com)

0311 GMT - South Korea's headline inflation likely rose above 3% in August, a poll shows. The median forecast from 13 economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal is for a 3.3% on-year rise in the benchmark consumer-price index, following a 2.8% rise in July. On a monthly basis, the index likely gained 0.4% in August. Deutsche Bank analysts say that elevated cost pressures continue to pass through, while improving income conditions are adding to demand-side pressures. The central bank has flagged an August inflation pickup partly due to base effects from telecommunication fee discounts offered by local mobile carriers a year earlier. The August CPI data are due on Wednesday. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0246 GMT - The Singapore dollar weakens slightly against its U.S. counterpart in Asia amid fading appetite for risky assets. "Renewed U.S.-Iran military exchanges rattled sentiment," UOB Global Economics & Markets Research says in a report. "Geopolitical risk remains elevated, with U.S.-Iran hostilities ongoing." The U.S. dollar is 0.1% higher at 1.2716 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0243 GMT - Barring further tightening by the Reserve Bank of Australia, the pace of monthly Australian house price falls will slow in the months ahead, with the housing market bottoming out early next year, says Abhijit Surya, senior economist at Capital Economics. Still, the outlook for monetary policy has become less certain, given that inflation is far too high for the RBA's liking, he adds. Continued upward pressure on rents won't help matters either, he says. If the RBA were to push ahead with further tightening, expect to see a steeper peak-to-trough fall, he adds. Capital Economics currently expects a 7% drop. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0239 GMT - Thailand's 2026 economic growth is likely to remain modest, despite a potentially stronger 3Q performance, Barclays economists say in a note. A recent Bank of Thailand report showed that the economy expanded in July from June, partly driven by government stimulus. The private consumption index rose 1.2% on month in July. However, Barclays notes that the rise in private consumption could be short-lived, as the government stimulus is set to conclude at the end of September. Barclays expects Thailand's economy to expand 2.2% in 2026, slower than the 2.4% expansion in 2025. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)
